'''Yirandhali''' (Yirandali, Jirandali), also known as '''Pooroga''',<ref>[http://www.ausanthrop.net/resources/ausanthrop_db/detail.php?id_search=169 Detailed record of the Jirandali], AusAnthrop Australian Aboriginal tribal database</ref> is an [[Australian Aboriginal language]] of [[Hughenden, Queensland|Hughenden]] in Central Queensland.<ref name="foundings">[http://foundingdocs.gov.au/pathways.html Foundingdocs website]</ref>  Yirandhali is a [[Pama–Nyungan]] language. Dixon (2002) speculates that it may belong in the [[Maric]] branch of that family, but further research is required before this can be verified, due to the limited lexical material that is available in the language.<ref name="Dixon">Dixon, Robert (2002) ''Australian Languages: Their Nature and Development''.  {{ISBN|0521473780}}.</ref><ref name="Koch, Harold 2004">Koch, Harold (2004), ''A methodological history of Australian linguistic classification''.  {{ISBN|9027247617}}</ref>

There is very little information available about the languages of this region. Oral recounts suggest that the town area of Hughenden was a place that was passed through rather than a place that was used as a regular campsite. The [[Flinders River]] is often a dry river bed.

At the nearby [[Porcupine Gorge]], in an area known locally as 'the Tattoos', there are signs of [[Rock drawing|Aboriginal rock drawings]]. This area would have been a more reliable source of water.

==Classification==
A [[Pama–Nyungan]] language, Dixon (2002) speculated that the language may belong in the [[Maric languages|Maric]] subfamily, and this is accepted in Bowern (2011),<ref>Bowern, Claire. 2011. "[http://anggarrgoon.wordpress.com/2011/12/23/how-many-languages-were-spoken-in-australia/ How Many Languages Were Spoken in Australia?]", ''Anggarrgoon: Australian languages on the web'', 23 December 2011 ([http://pamanyungan.sites.yale.edu/master-list-australian-languages-v12 corrected] 6 February 2012)</ref> but this cannot be verified, due to the limited lexical material available.<ref name="Dixon"/><ref name="Koch, Harold 2004"/>

== Phonology ==
One of the distinguishing features of the language is that every word ends with a [[vowel]] sound.  For instance, the root word ŋamun (breast) common in other languages of the region has been incorporated in Yirandali as "ŋamuna".<ref name="Dixon" />
